s: Ecclesiastes 4:9–12 — “Two are better than one, because together they get a good reward for their work.
If they fall, one will help the other up. But how sad for the one who is alone when he falls, because there is no one to help him up.
Also, if two lie down together, they keep warm. But how can one person keep warm alone?
If someone overpowers one of them, two can stand up against him. A rope of three strands does not snap quickly.”
There are many reasons why true Christianity has sadly grown weak. One of the biggest may be that we no longer meet together in religious groups.

So I want to do my part to encourage this excellent way of growing in godliness. I have chosen a Bible passage that comes from the experience of the wisest of men. If I explain it and illustrate it a little, it will fully serve my purpose. My purpose is to show, as well as I can, why people need each other in general, and why believers need religious groups in particular, and what good comes from them.
“Two are better than one,” and so on.
From these words I want to prove several things.
First, that the wise man is right when he says, “Two are better than one.” This is true of people living together in general, and of religious groups in particular.
Second, I will give some reasons why two are better than one, especially in religious groups.
1. Because people can help each other up when they slip: “If they fall, one will help the other up.”
2. Because they can give each other warmth: “Also, if two lie down together, they keep warm. But how can one person keep warm alone?”
3. Because they can protect each other from people who oppose them: “If someone overpowers one of them, two can stand up against him. A rope of three strands does not snap quickly.” From this,
Third, I will show the duty that every member of a religious group has.
And fourth, I will draw a lesson or two from what I have said. Then I will finish with a few words of encouragement.
First, I need to prove that the wise man is right that “two are better than one.” This is true of people living together in general, and of religious groups in particular.
What better way to prove it than to show that living together is absolutely necessary for the good of both our bodies and our souls?
If we think of man as he was when he first came from the hands of his Maker, we picture him as perfect and complete, lacking nothing.
But God's thoughts are not like our thoughts. He saw that something was still missing to make Adam happy.
And what was that?
Well, a helper suited to him.
This is what the Bible says: “And the Lord God said, ‘It is not good for the man to be by himself. I will make a helper suited to him.’”
Notice that God said, “It is not good.” This shows that creation would have been incomplete in some way unless a suitable helper was found for Adam.

That was man's situation before the fall. Even when he was perfect, he needed a helper. So how much more is this true since the fall! We come out of our mother's womb naked and helpless. Our needs grow as we get older. We can hardly get through a single day without helping each other. So we can truly say, “It is not good for man to be by himself.”
So we see that living together is absolutely necessary for our bodily and personal needs.
If we look further and think of mankind as divided into different cities, countries, and nations, this becomes even clearer.
How could communities hold together, or trade go on, without people working together?

It would be impossible. God, in his wise care, seems to have given almost every country its own special product. It is as if he did this on purpose, to make us need each other. He has joined all the parts of the human race together so wonderfully “that the eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I can do without you,’ and the hand cannot say to the foot, ‘I can do without you.’”
Many more examples could be given of how much we need each other for our bodies, our personal lives, and our nations.
But what are all these compared with the far greater need of our souls? When we weigh them on God's scales, they are nothing next to that need.
No doubt it was mainly because of the soul, this better part of us, that God said, “It is not good for the man to be by himself.”

Imagine Adam as happy as he could possibly be. He was placed in God's paradise as the lord of all creation. He spent all his hours worshiping and praising the blessed One who made him. Even so, his soul was an exact copy of God's nature, and it is part of God's nature to share itself. So, apart from God's own all-sufficiency, Adam could not be completely happy. He was alone and had no one to share himself with. He could not even be content in paradise, because he had no partner in his joys.
God knew this. That is why he said, “It is not good for the man to be by himself. I will make a helper suited to him.”

It is true that this became the fatal cause of his fall. But that was not because living with others naturally leads to sin. Partly it was because of that cursed rebel who cunningly lies in wait to deceive. And partly it was Adam's own foolishness. He chose to be miserable with the one he loved rather than trust God to give him another wife.
Think about the close friendship with heaven that our first father could enjoy while he was still innocent. We might think his soul needed company as little as we first imagined his body did.
But God and the holy angels were so far above him, and the animals so far below him. So nothing could compare with having someone to talk with who was “bone of his bone and flesh of his flesh.”
So we see that man could not be fully happy without a companion of his own kind, even in paradise. How much less can he be happy now that he has been driven out!

Let us look at man a little as he is by nature now, since the fall. His “understanding is darkened, and his mind is cut off from the life of God.” He can no more see the way he should go than a blind man can describe the sun. Even so, he must receive his sight before he can see God. And if he never sees God, he can never be happy.
Let us look at him in this light (or rather, this darkness). Then let us try to deny that we need each other, if we can.
We find that we absolutely need God to reveal his will to us. By nature we are just as unable to know our duty as we are to do it.
And how can we learn unless someone teaches us?
But if God taught us himself, wouldn't we, like Moses, tremble and shake with fear?
And if angels were sent to teach us, that would be far too frightening as well.
So it is necessary (at least, the way God deals with us shows this) that we be drawn with human cords—“with the cords of a man.”
And now that God has given his revelation, we should help one another, under God. We should teach each other what we need to know for our eternal peace, and urge each other to put it into practice.
Without doubt, this is the main purpose God has had for people living together since the fall. And it is a strong reason why “two are better than one,” and why we should “not abandon our gatherings.”
But let us go further. Let us think of ourselves as Christians. God's Holy Spirit has helped to take this natural blindfold partly off our eyes, so we can now see what he wants from us.

Suppose we have, in some small way, tasted the good word of life. Suppose we have felt the powers of the world to come shaping our souls toward God. Suppose we are fully and deeply convinced of these things: We are soldiers enlisted under the flag of Christ. At our baptism we openly declared war against the world, the flesh, and the devil. We have perhaps often renewed that promise by taking the Lord's Supper. We are surrounded by millions of enemies outside us, and a whole army of enemies has infected us inside. We are commanded to shine like lights in the world, among people who are crooked and twisted. We are traveling toward a long eternity, and we need every possible help to show us the way and encourage us as we go.
I say, let us think about all this. Then, my brothers, how each of us will cry out, “How necessary it is to meet together in religious groups!”
The first Christians understood this very well. That is why we find them always keeping up their fellowship with one another. What does the Bible say?
They faithfully kept on in the apostles' teaching and in fellowship, Acts 2:42.
As soon as the great council let Peter and John go, they hurried back to their friends.
“When they were set free, they went back to their own people and told them everything the high priest had said to them,” Acts 4:23.
As soon as Paul was converted, he “stayed three days with the disciples in Damascus.”
Acts 9:19. And later, when Peter was set free from prison, he went straight to Mary's house, where “great crowds had gathered and were praying,” Acts 12:12.
We are also told that Christians in later times used to meet before daylight to sing a psalm to Christ as God.
That is how precious the fellowship of believers was in those days.
Someone may ask, “What good will we get from doing this now?”
My answer is: a great deal, in every way.

“Two are better than one, because together they get a good reward for their work. If they fall, one will help the other up. But how sad for the one who is alone when he falls, because there is no one to help him up.
Also, if two lie down together, they keep warm. But how can one person keep warm alone?
If someone overpowers one of them, two can stand up against him. A rope of three strands does not snap quickly.”
This leads me straight to my second main point. Here I was to give some reasons why “two are better than one,” especially in religious groups.

1. In our present condition we cannot always stand up straight. Because our nature is weak, we are bound to fall. So one important reason why two are better than one—in other words, one great advantage of a religious group—is this: “When they fall, one will help the other up.”
And what an excellent reason this is!

Sadly, we easily fall into wrong thinking and wrong living. We are unable, or at least very unwilling, to notice or correct our own mistakes. The world is quick to flatter us about our faults, and very few people are kind enough to tell us the truth. When we think about all this, what a priceless gift it must be to have a group of true, wise, warm-hearted friends around us! They keep watching over our souls. They tell us where we have fallen, and they warn us not to fall again.
It is such a great gift that (to quote a well-known Christian) we will never know how valuable it is until we get to glory.

But that is not all. Suppose we could always stand up straight. Even then, anyone who thinks about how hard it is to live a godly life, and about how easily he himself becomes lukewarm and careless, will see something more. He must be eager as well as steady if he ever hopes to enter the kingdom of heaven.
So here the wise man shows us another excellent reason why two are better than one:
“Also, if two lie down together, they keep warm. But how can one person keep warm alone?”
That was the next thing to look at.
2. A second reason why two are better than one is that they can give each other warmth.
Everyone knows it, and it is true: burning coals soon go out if you spread them apart. But if you pile them together, they make each other burn brighter and give off heat that lasts.
The same is true in the case we are talking about.

When Christians who have been set on fire by God's grace stay together, they make each other burn brighter. But if they separate and stay apart, it is no surprise if they soon cool down and become lukewarm.
If two or three meet together in Christ's name, they will have warmth. But how can one person keep warm alone?
Notice the words: “How can one person keep warm alone?”
The wise man puts this as a question. That shows it is impossible, or at least very hard, to stay warm in your faith without company, when company is available.
So here is another excellent benefit that comes from religious groups: they keep us eager as well as steady in living a godly life.
Let me explain this a little more by giving a comparison or two.

As I mentioned before, let us think of ourselves as soldiers enlisted under Christ's flag. We are going out with “ten thousand to face an enemy coming against us with twenty thousand.” We are people who must “wrestle not only against flesh and blood, but against rulers, against powers, and against spiritual evil in high places.”

Then tell me, all of you who fear God: isn't it a priceless gift to have a company of fellow soldiers always around us? They cheer each other on and urge each other to stand firm, to stay in line, and to follow bravely the captain of our salvation—even if it means going through a sea of blood.

Let us look at ourselves in another way I mentioned earlier. We are travelers heading toward a long eternity. God's free grace has, in part, rescued us from our natural slavery in Egypt. Now we are marching through the wilderness of this world, led by our spiritual Joshua, to the land of our heavenly Canaan.
Let us also think about how easily we are frightened by every difficulty. We cry out, “There are lions!
There are lions in the way!
There are the sons of Anak” to fight before we can take the promised land.

How quick we are, like Lot's wife, to look back longingly at our spiritual Sodom! Or, like the foolish Israelites, we long again for the pots of meat in Egypt, and we want to go back to our old natural life of slavery.

Think about this, my brothers. Then see what a blessed gift it will be to have true Israelites around us. They will always remind us how foolish any such cowardly plan would be. And they will remind us of the terrible misery we will fall into if we come even a little short of the promised land.
More could be said about this, but the limits of a sermon like this make me hurry on.
3. Here is a third reason why two are better than one, which the wise man mentions in the text: they can protect each other from enemies outside.
“If someone overpowers one of them, two can stand up against him. A rope of three strands does not snap quickly.”

So far we have looked at how religious groups greatly protect us from falling into sin and lukewarmness (or at least from falling dangerously). And we have seen this in relation to our own sinful nature.
But what does the wise son of Sirach say?

“My son, when you set out to serve the Lord, get your soul ready for temptation.” That temptation comes not only from enemies inside us but also from enemies outside us. It comes especially from our two great enemies, the world and the devil. As soon as you turn your eyes toward heaven, the world will immediately try to turn them another way. It will tell you that you don't need to be different from everyone else to be religious. It will say you can be a Christian without leaving the ordinary road so far behind.
The devil, too, will be busy with his clever hints and wicked suggestions. He will try to distract you or scare you so that you stop pressing forward “to take hold of the crown of life.”

If he cannot win that way, he will try another. To make his temptation harder to notice, and so more successful, he may use some of your closest relatives or most powerful friends (just as he used Peter against our blessed Master). They will keep telling you to go easy on yourself. They will say you don't need to try so hard. They will tell you that getting to heaven is not as difficult as some people make it sound, and the way is not as narrow as others think.

But see how helpful religious friends are! Suppose you find yourself surrounded like this on every side, and you cannot resist such terrible advice (even though it seems friendly). Then hurry to your companions. They will teach you a truer and better lesson. They will tell you that you must be different if you want to be truly religious. They will tell you that a Christian can no more be hidden than a city built on a hill. They will say that if you want to be an almost-Christian (which is as good as being none at all), you can live the same lazy, careless life you see most other people living. But if you want to be not just almost but completely a Christian, they will tell you that you must go much further. You must not just seek weakly, but “strive with all your might to get in through the narrow gate.” There is still only one way to heaven, just as there always was: through the narrow passage of a real conversion. And to bring about this mighty work, you must keep up a steady but necessary discipline of fasting, watching, and prayer.

So the only reason those friends give you such advice is that they are not willing to work so hard themselves. Or, as our Savior told Peter at a similar time, it is because they “do not care about the things of God, but about the things of men.”
So this is another excellent blessing that comes from religious groups: friends can protect each other from those who oppose them.
The devil knows this very well. That is why he has always done everything he can to crush and stop the fellowship of believers.
This was his great trick when the gospel was first planted: he persecuted those who believed it, in order to split them up.
God, as he always will, turned it to good. But it still shows how much the devil hates it when Christians meet together.
And he has not given up his old plan. He usually tries to get us alone so he can tempt us. When we are without each other's help, he hopes to lead us captive to do whatever he wants.

He knows that his own cause grows stronger when people gather. So first he tries to convince us to neglect the fellowship of believers. Then he tells us to “stand in the way of sinners,” hoping that this will bring us at last into the seat of the mockers.
Judas and Peter are sad examples of this.

As soon as Judas left the other disciples at supper, he went out and betrayed his Master. And Peter's terrible fall, when he dared to go among a crowd of enemies, clearly shows what the devil will try to do when he gets us alone.
If Peter had stayed with his own friends, he might have stayed faithful. But sadly, how quickly that single cord was broken!
Our blessed Savior knew this very well. That is why it is worth noticing that he always sent out his disciples “two by two.”

So after seeing so many benefits that come from religious groups, don't we have good reason to cry out with the wise man in my text, “How sad for the one who is alone! When he falls, there is no one to help him up!”
When he is cold, he has no friend to warm him. When he is attacked, he has no partner to help him fight off his enemy.
III. Now I come to my third main point. Here I was to show the duties that every member of a religious group has as a member. There are three.
1. Correcting each other; 2.
Encouraging each other; 3. Helping and defending each other.
1. Correcting each other. “Two are better than one, because when they fall, one will help the other up.”

Correction can be understood in a wider sense. Then it means gently helping a brother get back up when he falls into sin or error. Or it can be understood in a narrower sense. Then it only covers the small mistakes that even the holiest people alive cannot avoid.
The wise man in the text assumes that all of us can fall in both ways: “When they fall (which means any of us may fall), one will help the other up.”

From this we can conclude that “when a brother is caught in a fault, the one who is spiritual (that is, born again, and aware of how sinful and weak human nature is) should restore that person with a gentle spirit.”
The apostle gives the reason why he should do this: “Think of yourself, in case you are tempted too.” In other words, remember how weak you are, or you may fall to the same kind of temptation.
We are all weak and unsteady creatures. The only reason we do not run into the same wild sins as other people is God's free grace and his good care over us.
So every brother who does wrong deserves our pity, not our anger. And each member should try to be the first, and also the gentlest, in helping him back to where he was before.
But suppose someone was not just caught off guard, but chose to commit a serious sin. Even then, who are you to refuse to forgive your brother who has done wrong?
“Let anyone who stands be careful that he does not fall.”
My brothers, take the holy apostles as great examples. Learn from them how you should act in this matter.
Think how quickly they welcomed Peter back into fellowship, even though he had so deliberately denied his Master. We find John and Peter together only two days later, John 20:2.
And in verse 19 we find him gathered with the rest.
That is how quickly they forgave their brother, who had sinned but was now sorry. That is how quickly they welcomed him back among them.
“Let us go and do the same.”
But every member of a religious group has another kind of correction to give. This is a gentle warning about some mistake that is not actually a sin but could lead to sin.

This seems easier, but it may actually turn out to be harder than the first kind. When a person has really sinned, he has to admit that his brothers are right to correct him. But when it is only about some small misstep, the pride in our nature will hardly let us put up with (endure, tolerate) it.
This medicine may taste bitter to our brother. But if we care at all about his good, some friendly hand must give it to him.
So by all means, give it. But be like a skilled doctor: coat the bitter pill, and try, if you can, to trick your brother into getting healthy and well.
“Let all bitterness, anger, spite, and evil talk be put away” from it.
Let the patient know that the only goal is his recovery, and that you take no pleasure in hurting your brother for no reason. Then you cannot fail.
2. The second duty that comes from the words of the text is encouraging each other:
“Also, if two lie down together, they keep warm.”

Notice that the wise man thinks it is impossible for religious people to meet together and not be warmer because of each other's company. It is just as impossible as two people lying in the same bed and still freezing with cold.
But how can we pass warmth to each other unless we stir up God's gift in one another by encouraging each other as brothers?

So let every member of a religious group write this advice from that zealous apostle on his heart: “Make sure you encourage one another and push each other toward love and good works, and do it even more as you see the day of the Lord getting closer.”

Believe me, my brothers, we need encouragement. It wakes up our sleepy souls. It puts us on guard against the temptations of the world, the flesh, and the devil. It moves us to deny ourselves, take up our crosses, and follow our blessed Master and the glorious company of saints and martyrs, “who through faith fought the good fight and have gone ahead of us to receive what God promised.”

So it seems necessary to spend a third of the time when a religious group meets on this important duty. What good does it do to have our minds enlightened by devotional reading, unless at the same time our wills are moved and set on fire by encouraging each other to put it into practice?

Also, this is the best way both to receive light and to give it. It is the only way to keep and increase the warmth and heat each person brought with him at first. God has arranged this, as he has with all other spiritual gifts: “To the one who has—that is, who uses and shares what he has—more will be given. But from the one who has not, or who does not use the heat he has, even what he seemed to have will be taken away.”
That is how needed, how truly necessary, encouragement is for the good of the group.
3. Third, the text points to another duty of every member of a religious group: to defend each other from those who oppose them.
“If someone overpowers one of them, two can stand up against him. A rope of three strands does not snap quickly.”
Here the wise man takes it for granted that attacks and stumbling blocks will come—and even that they may win.
And this is exactly what our blessed Master told us long ago.
That does not mean there is anything in Christianity itself that could cause or encourage such trouble in the slightest. No! In fact, Christianity breathes nothing but unity and love.

But ever since the fatal sentence God spoke after our first parents fell—“I will make your descendants and hers enemies of each other”—it has been this way. The one born of the flesh, the sinner who has not been born again or converted, has in every age “persecuted the one born of the Spirit.” And it will always be so.
We see an early example of this in Cain and Abel, in Ishmael and Isaac, and in Jacob and Esau.
In fact, the whole Bible is almost nothing but a history of the great, ongoing conflict between the children of this world and the children of God.

The first Christians were striking examples of this. Thank God, those troubled times are now over. Yet the apostle has given it as a general rule, and everyone who is sincere finds out by experience that it is true: “Those who are determined to live godly lives in Christ Jesus must (in one way or another, until the end of the world) suffer persecution.”
So, to keep this from making us abandon our blessed Master's cause, every member should join forces to stand against it.

To do this better, each person would do well to share his experiences, troubles, and temptations from time to time. He should first ask for God's help, since without it everything is worthless. Then he should ask his companions to correct, encourage, or comfort him, whatever his situation needs. That way, “if one cannot win against it, two can stand up against it. A rope of three strands will not snap quickly—much less a rope of many strands.”
IV. But it is time for me to move on to the fourth main point I promised: to draw a lesson or two from what I have said.
1. First, if “two are better than one,” and religious groups bring so many great benefits, then every true Christian has a duty to start, build up, and support groups like this, as much as he can.
And I believe we can boldly say this: if a spirit of true Christianity is ever revived in the world, it will have to come about through something like this.

Surely we have plenty of reasons to push us into this good and necessary work. Suppose everything I have said so far had no weight at all. Even so, I think one fact alone should be enough: a great part of our happiness in heaven will be the fellowship of God's people. Or this fact: those who disagree with us grow stronger in their cause and their devotion through nothing so much as their frequent meetings. Either one of these facts, I say, should move us to do our very best to follow their good example and set up a lasting, godly fellowship of believers here on earth.
Add to this that we see the kingdom of darkness being built up every day by these same methods. So shouldn't the kingdom of Christ be set up against it?
Will the wicked children of Belial meet together and strengthen each other in evil, while the children of God do not unite and strengthen each other in godliness?
Will club after club be supported for partying late into the night and spreading vice, while hardly one group can be found for spreading goodness?
Be amazed at this, O heavens!

2. But this leads me to a second lesson. I must warn people about the great danger they are in if they support groups that are completely opposed to religion, whether by giving money, by attending, or by approving of them.

I don't mean only those public gatherings that are clearly meant for nothing but wild parties and feasting, for sexual sin and immoral behavior, where even a decent pagan would be ashamed to be seen. I also mean those entertainments and gatherings that seem innocent, which fashionable people love so much and spend so much time on. Yet they keep just as many people from really caring about true religion as drunkenness, immoral living, or any other sins do.
Of course, while we are in this world, we need proper rest and recreation. It helps prepare us for both our work and our religion.

But think about people who call themselves Christians. At their baptism they solemnly promised to turn their backs on the empty things of this sinful world. The Bible commands them “to avoid anything that even looks like evil, and to live as citizens of heaven.” For people like this to support gatherings that are (to say the least) empty and silly, and that naturally pull our minds away from God, is foolish, ridiculous, and sinful.
Surely two are not better than one in this case! No, we should wish that not even one person could be found taking part in it.
The sooner we stop meeting together in this way, the better. And the sooner the cord that holds such groups together is broken, the better—even if it were a thousand strands thick.

But you, my brothers, did not learn Christ that way. Instead, like true disciples of your Lord and Master, you have by God's blessing (as this evening's solemn service clearly shows) happily formed yourselves into such groups. If you faithfully attend them and make good use of them, they are sure to strengthen you in your Christian battle, and “make you fruitful in every good word and work.”

What is left for me to do, as I planned, except first to close what I have said with a few words of encouragement? I beg you, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to keep going in the way you have started. Keep attending your groups faithfully and conscientiously. In this way, discourage vice, encourage goodness, and build each other up in the knowledge and fear of God.

Please let me “stir up your pure minds by reminding you.” And let me urge you, “if there is any comfort in Christ, any fellowship of the Spirit,” to think about this again and again: all Christians in general, and all members of religious groups in particular, are in a special way like houses built on a hill. So it matters very much that you live carefully in front of those who are outside the faith. Watch yourselves, so that the way you live every day fits such an open and special profession of the gospel of Christ. Remember that everyone's eyes are on you, closely examining every detail of how you act. And every public, deliberate wrong done by any single member will, to some degree, bring shame and dishonor on your whole brotherhood.

So work hard, my dear brothers, to make your actions match what you say you believe. And don't think it will be enough to say on the last day, Lord, didn't we meet together in your name and cheer each other on by singing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs?

For I tell you the truth: in spite of all this, our blessed Lord will tell you to go away from him. In fact, you will receive a terrible condemnation if, in the middle of all these big claims, you are found to be people who do evil.
But God forbid that anything so evil should happen to you! May there never be a Judas, a traitor, among such outstanding followers of our common Master.

No! In fact, I am persuaded otherwise. The excellence of your rule, the regularity of your meetings, and especially your devoted zeal in gathering so publicly and solemnly so often each year make me believe that you want not just to seem Christians, but to really be Christians. And I believe you hope to be found on the last day to be what you want people to think you are now: holy, sincere disciples of a crucified Redeemer.
Oh, may you always stay this way!
Make it your daily, constant goal, by both your words and your example, to fill all your dealings with others—especially with those in your own groups—with this same most blessed spirit and attitude.

In this way you will make the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ beautiful in every way. In this way you will get a foretaste of the happiness of the life to come. And by taking part in and making good use of the fellowship of believers on earth, you will be made ready to join the fellowship of the spirits of righteous people made perfect, of the holy angels—yes, of the ever-blessed and eternal God in heaven.

May God in his infinite mercy grant this through Jesus Christ our Lord. To him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, three persons and one God, be given all honor and praise, might, majesty, and power, as is most fitting, now and forever. Amen.

Why is there so little love among Christians? Love is the very sign by which everyone should know that we are followers of the holy Jesus. So why has it almost disappeared from the Christian world? If we look into it, we will find that a big part of the reason is this: we neglect intercession, or we do it in a shallow way. Intercession is a wonderful part of prayer. It means asking God to show his grace and mercy to other people.

Some people forget to pray for others because they hardly ever remember to pray for themselves. And even those who faithfully pray to their Father in heaven are often selfish when they come before God's throne of grace. They do not widen their prayers to include the good of their fellow Christians as they should. Because of this, they fall short of true Christian love, a sincere love for their brothers and sisters. Their holy calling as Christians requires them to reach for that love. Without it, even if they gave away everything they owned to feed the poor, and even gave their bodies to be burned, it would do them no good at all.
Since this is how things are, I will use the words of my text to try to show you three things. (Those words were first meant in a narrower way.)
I. First, that every Christian has a duty to pray for others as well as for himself.
II. Second, whom we should pray for, and how we should do it. And,
III. Third, I will give some reasons that should move all Christians to do much more of this great duty of praying for others.
I. First, then, I will try to show that every Christian has a duty to pray for others, as well as for himself.

Prayer is a duty that even natural religion teaches. Even the heathen never neglected it, though many among us who are Christians in name but heathen in practice do. Prayer is so essential to being a Christian that you could just as well expect to find a living man who does not breathe as a true Christian who does not have the spirit of prayer and pleading with God.
That is why, as soon as St. Paul was converted, the Lord Almighty said, "Look, he is praying."
And it will be the same with every child of God as soon as he becomes one. Prayer has rightly been called the natural cry of a newborn soul.
In the heart of every true believer there is a pull toward heaven, a divine attraction. It draws him to talk with God just as clearly as a magnet pulls a needle.

True believers feel deeply how weak they are and how full Christ is. They are strongly convinced that their nature is corrupt and that they need God's grace to make them new. This will not let them rest. They cry out day and night to their Almighty Redeemer. They ask that God's image, which they lost in Adam, would be begun in them, carried forward, and made fully complete in both soul and body. They ask this through Christ's all-powerful work as their go-between, and through the work of his blessed Spirit, who makes them holy.

That is how earnest and persistent all sincere Christians are when they pray for themselves. But they do not feel the needs of their Christian brothers and sisters as strongly, as deeply, or as constantly. So, for the most part, they are too careless and weak in their prayers for them.

But suppose the love of God were poured into our hearts. Suppose we loved our neighbor the way the Son of God, our Savior, loved us, as he commanded and showed us. Then we could not help praying just as hard for their good, both for their souls and for their daily lives, as for our own. We would long and work just as hard for others to share in the blessings of Jesus Christ's suffering and death as for ourselves.

No one should think this is some rare kind of love, a high level of perfection that only a few can reach. We are all commanded to "love our neighbor (that is, every person) as ourselves." We are even told to "lay down our lives for our brothers and sisters." So it is everyone's duty to pray for their neighbors as much as for themselves. At all times, by every act and word of love and kindness, we should show that we are ready even to give our lives for them, if God should ever call us to do it.

Our blessed Savior "gave us an example, so that we would follow in his steps" in everything else, and he did so especially in this. Just before his suffering, he prayed a divine, perfect prayer that no one could ever equal. It is recorded in John 17. In it we find only a few requests for himself, but many for the good of his disciples. He also gave us a perfect pattern for prayer. In it he teaches us to say, not "My Father," but "Our Father." This reminds us that whenever we come before God's throne of grace, we should not pray only for ourselves, but for all our brothers and sisters in Christ.
So praying for others is clearly a duty for every Christian.
II. Next we must think about whom we should pray for, and how we should do it.
1. First, our prayers for others must include everyone.
The apostle says, "I want prayers, requests, and intercessions to be made for all people."
God's mercy is over everything he has made. Jesus Christ died to rescue a people out of every nation and language. So we should pray that "all people may come to know the truth and be saved."

The Holy Scriptures contain many precious promises that the gospel will be preached through the whole world. They say that "the earth will be covered with the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea." So it is our duty not to limit our prayers to our own country. We should pray that all the nations who now sit in darkness and in the shadow of death would have the glorious gospel shine on them, just as it shines on us.

But you do not need anyone to teach you this. God himself, and Jesus Christ himself, have taught you to pray that his kingdom would come. Part of what that request means is that "God's ways may be known on earth, and his saving power among all nations."

2. Next to praying for all people, St. Paul tells us to pray for kings. We should pray especially for our present ruler, King George, and for everyone who holds authority under him. We pray this so that we may live quiet lives, full of godliness and honesty.

Think how heavy the load of governing is. Think how much the well-being of any people depends on the zeal and godly lives of those who rule over them. Picture the many dangers and difficulties that rulers face because of their position, and the constant temptations they face to live in luxury and please themselves. Then we will not only feel sorry for them, but pray for them. God kept Esther, David, and Josiah "unstained by the world" in the middle of the splendor of a royal court, and he gave success to their plans. We will ask him to keep our rulers holy and blameless in the same way, and to bless all the work of their hands. But
3. Third, you should pray in a very special way for those whom "the Holy Spirit has made overseers over you."

St. Paul asks this again and again of the churches he writes to. In our text he says, "Brothers and sisters, pray for us." And in his letter to the Ephesians he says, "Pray at all times, with every kind of request. And pray for me too, that I may open my mouth boldly and announce the mystery of the gospel."

In another place he shows how earnest this request is and how much their prayers mean to him. He tells the church to "strive together with him in their prayers." (The word he used in the original language means to be in agony.)

The great St. Paul was God's chosen instrument and a favorite of heaven. Yet he needed his converts to pray for him with all their might. If that is true, then surely ordinary ministers of the gospel need the prayers of their own congregations even more.

I must press this part of your duty on you in a very special way, because it matters so much. No doubt many people often miss out on much good because they neglect to pray for their ministers. They would have received that good if they had prayed for them as they should.
And that is not to mention that people often complain that there are not enough hard-working and faithful pastors.
But how can people deserve good pastors if they will not pray earnestly to God for them?
If we will not pray to the Lord of the harvest, how can we expect him to send workers into his harvest?
Besides, how ungrateful it is not to pray for your ministers!
They keep watch and work hard, preaching and teaching for you and for your salvation. Shouldn't you pray for them in return?

If someone does something kind for your body, you think it is right and proper, and your clear duty, to pray for them. So shouldn't you remember in your prayers those who feed and nourish your souls every day?
On top of all this, praying for your ministers clearly shows that you believe this: Paul may plant and Apollos may water, but only God makes things grow.

You will also find that it is the best way to do yourself good. In answer to your prayers, God may give them a double portion of his Holy Spirit. Then they will be better equipped to give you a fuller knowledge of spiritual things. They will also be able to handle the word of truth with more skill.

People should always follow this advice. When their ministers pray to God on their behalf, they should humbly ask God to grant all those requests. When their ministers speak to them on God's behalf, they should pray that the Holy Spirit would come down on everyone who hears the word. If people did this, we would see their teaching do more visible good. We would also see more love between ministers and their people.
The people's prayers would then hold up their ministers' hands. And people will never dare to insult or slander those they are always praying for.
4. After our ministers, our friends deserve a place in our prayers. But we should not be satisfied with praying for them in general terms. We should fit our prayers to their particular situations.
When God struck Miriam with leprosy, Moses cried out, "Lord, heal her."
And when the nobleman came to ask Jesus Christ for help for his child, he said, "Lord, my little daughter is close to death. I beg you, come and heal her."
In the same way, when our friends are going through hard times, we should try to pray for them with their particular troubles in mind.
For example, is a friend sick?

We should pray that, if God is willing, the sickness will not end in death. But if God wills otherwise, we should pray that he will give our friend grace to accept this trial in such a way that, when this painful life is over, he may live with God forever.
Is a friend unsure about an important matter?

We should bring his case before God, as Moses did with the case of the daughters of Zelophehad. We should pray that God's Holy Spirit will lead him into all truth and give him the guidance he needs at the right time.
Is he poor and in need?
We should pray that his faith will never fail, and that God will help him when the right time comes.

In every other situation too, we should not pray for our friends only in general. We should fit our prayers to their particular sufferings and troubles. Otherwise, we might never ask for the very things our friends need most.

It is true that praying this way will often force some people to set aside the written prayers they usually use. But if we get used to it, and feel deeply what we are asking for, even people with no education will not be short of the right words.

The Bible gives us many great examples of how well this kind of specific prayer works. But none is more remarkable than the story of Abraham's servant in the book of Genesis. He was sent to find a wife for Abraham's son Isaac, and he prayed for him in a very specific way.
The rest of the story tells us how remarkably his prayer was answered.

If Christians today prayed for their friends in the same specific way, and with the same faith, as Abraham's servant did for his master, they would no doubt often receive answers just as clear. They would have just as much reason to thank God for them as he did. But
5. Just as we should pray for our friends, we must also pray for our enemies.
Jesus Christ says, "Bless those who curse you, and pray for those who treat you cruelly and persecute you."

He backed up this command in the strongest way by his own example. In the very agony and pain of death, he prayed even for the people who were killing him: "Father, forgive them, because they do not understand what they are doing!"

It must be admitted that this is a hard duty. But it is not impossible for those who have given up the things of this life. (All hatred between people comes from loving those things too much.) They know the terrible warnings given against those who cause Christ's little ones to stumble. So, out of real pity and concern for the danger those people are in, they can pray for the ones who cause such harm.

6. Finally, to finish this point: we should pray for everyone who is suffering in any way, whether in mind, body, or circumstances. We should pray for all who want and need our prayers, and for all who do not pray for themselves.
Oh, how I wish that everyone who hears me would set aside some time every day to carry out this most necessary duty properly!
To help you do that,
I will now go on
III. To show you the benefits of praying for others every day, and to give you some reasons that should move you to do it. And
1. First, it will fill your hearts with love for one another.

Someone who prays with all his heart for all people every day at the throne of grace cannot help being filled with love and kindness toward everyone before long. As he keeps practicing love in this way, his heart will grow bigger without his even noticing. He will come to share in the overflowing love that is in Christ Jesus our Lord!

Envy, spite, revenge, and other hellish attitudes like them can never stay long in the heart of a person of grace who prays for others. Instead, he will be filled with joy, peace, gentleness, patience, and all the other gifts of the Holy Spirit.
By often bringing his neighbor's needs to God, he will come to feel those needs as if they were his own. He will rejoice with those who rejoice and cry with those who cry.
When others are blessed, he will not feel envy. Instead, he will see each blessing as an answer to his own prayers for them. And it will fill his soul with a joy too great for words, full of glory.

So pray for others often, both for everyone in general and for specific people. When you hear about your neighbor's faults, do not tell others about them or put them on display. Instead, bring them to God in private, and ask him to correct them and set them right.

When you hear about someone who is known for his sins, do not think you are right to be angry. Instead, ask Jesus Christ to convert him and make him a living reminder of his free grace. You cannot imagine what a wonderful change this habit will make in your heart! You will grow day by day in a spirit of love and gentleness toward all people!
But there is more. To encourage you to keep practicing this duty of praying for others, think about the many examples in the Bible that show how powerful and effective it is.
The Bible records great and wonderful things that happened because of this holy work.
It has stopped plagues. It has opened and shut the sky. And it has often turned God's anger away from his people.
Think how Abimelech's household was set free from the disease God sent on them when Abraham prayed for them!
When "Phinehas stood up and prayed," how quickly the plague stopped!
When Daniel humbled himself in sorrow and prayed for the Lord's own people, how quickly an angel was sent to tell him "his prayer was heard!"

And to give just one more example: Moses was praying for his people after they had worshiped idols. And God speaks as if Moses' persistent pleading had almost overpowered him. "Leave me alone," God says!

This is enough to show that praying for others is, I could almost say, all-powerful. It shows how we can wrestle with God like Jacob did, and with a holy kind of force win blessings both for ourselves and for others.

No doubt God has still spared this terribly sinful nation because of the hidden, powerful prayers of the few righteous people who are still among us. If there were not some faithful people like Moses left to stand in the gap, we would soon be destroyed, just like Sodom, and burned to ashes like Gomorrah.

But here is another reason to stir you up to pray for others. Very likely, this is something even the saints in glory often do. They have been set free from the burden of the body. They have been brought into the glorious freedom of God's children. But their happiness cannot be fully complete until the resurrection on the last day, when all their brothers and sisters will be glorified with them. So we can only think that they often plead with our heavenly Father to soon complete the number of his chosen people and to hurry the coming of his kingdom.
So shouldn't we who are on earth often join in this holy work with that glorious company, the spirits of good people who have been made perfect?

Our happiness in heaven will depend so much on the fellowship of the saints in the victorious church above. So shouldn't we often pray for the church that is still fighting its battles here below? Shouldn't we earnestly ask that we may all be one, just as the holy Jesus and his Father are one, so that we too may be made perfectly one?

To move you to this great work of love, remember this: it is what the holy and highly exalted Jesus himself does without ever stopping. He sits at the right hand of God, hears all our prayers, and always prays for us!
So someone who keeps praying for others is doing on earth what the eternal Son of God is always doing in heaven.

So when you lift up holy hands to pray for one another, imagine that you see heaven opened. Imagine you see the Son of God in all his glory, the great High Priest who brings you salvation. He stands before the throne of his heavenly Father and pleads for you. He points to his sacrifice, which is fully enough to cover everything!
So join your prayers to his. Ask him to make them rise through him like incense, and to have them received like a sweet fragrance that pleases God!

Picturing this will strengthen your faith. It will make your prayers earnest and holy. It will make you wrestle with God like Jacob, who saw God face to face and yet lived. You will wrestle like Abraham when he pleaded for Sodom. And you will wrestle like Jesus Christ himself, who, the night before his bitter suffering, was in agony and prayed even more earnestly.
And now, brothers and sisters, what more can I say? Jesus Christ himself has taught you to be rich in love, and in this good work of praying for one another.
Even if you are very lowly, even if you are as poor as Lazarus, you will then do good to all people. Thousands, even twenty times ten thousand, will be blessed because of you!

And after you have spent a few years in this holy work here, you will be taken up to that happy place where you have so often wished others could go. There, in the kingdom of his heavenly Father, you will be lifted up to sit at the right hand of the one who prays for us, who is all-powerful and always wins his case.

But I must urge this on you especially now. Most likely, none of you I have been preaching to here will ever see me again. I am now leaving you, trusting that God's most Holy Spirit is guiding me, and I do not know what will happen to me. So I need you to pray for me as hard as you can. Pray that nothing will turn me away from my duty. Pray that I will "not value even my own life, as long as I can finish my race with joy, and the work the Lord Jesus gave me, to tell the good news of God's grace!"

While I have been here, as far as I know, I have not failed to tell you the whole will of God. To some, my preaching may have been a smell of death that leads to death. But I trust that to others it has been a fragrance of life that leads to life. So I earnestly hope those people will not forget to remember me in their prayers.

As for me, you have shown me so much kindness that I did not deserve, and I cannot forget you. So I trust that my cry will rise to God even from the deep. While the winds and storms blow over me, I will pray to the Lord for you.

For in only a little while, "we must all stand before the judgment seat of Christ." There I must give a strict account of what I have preached, and you must give an account of how you have grown under it.
Oh, may I never be called as a quick witness against any of you whose salvation I have longed and worked for! I have done it sincerely, though far too weakly.

It is true that some people have accused me of acting from bad and selfish motives. "But it matters very little to me if I am judged by human judgment." I hope my motives are pure. But I beg you, brothers and sisters, by the mercies of God in Christ Jesus, pray that they will become even purer!
And pray that, as God's grace increases in me, I will grow in knowing and loving God through Jesus Christ our Lord.
And now, brothers and sisters, what more can I say?
I wish I could keep speaking much longer, because I can never fully express how much my soul longs for you!

So finally, brothers and sisters, "whatever is holy, whatever is pure, whatever is honest, whatever is well spoken of; if there is any comfort in Christ, if there is any fellowship of the Spirit," if there is any hope that we will meet each other with joy before the solemn judgment seat of Jesus Christ, "think about the things you have heard." Think about what your pastors have told you and will still tell you. Keep sitting under their ministry, and "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling." Then, whether I never see you again or God brings me back to you some day, I will always have the joy of knowing that you live in a way that "fits the gospel of Christ."

I have almost convinced myself that I would gladly suffer anything, if it could help in any way to save your precious souls, which will live forever. And I beg you, as my last request, "obey those who lead you in the Lord." Always be ready to listen to their preaching, as it is your clear duty to do.

Do not think that I want to be praised at the cost of anyone else's good name. Instead, remember this: do not admire any one person too much. But hold all your ministers in high regard and love them, as they rightly deserve because of their work.

And now, "brothers and sisters, I place you in God's hands, and in the care of the word of his grace. That word has power to build you up and to give you a share of the inheritance among all who are made holy."
May God reward you for everything you have done out of faith and all your hard work of love. May he help you do more and more of every good thing, in word and action, for all people.
May he truly turn to himself all who have been made aware of their sin, and wake up all who are dead in their wrongdoing and sins!
May he make everyone who is wavering strong and steady!

And may you all keep growing from one level of grace to the next, until you reach the full maturity of Christ. May you in this way become ready to stand before God, "in whose presence there is complete joy, and at whose right hand there are pleasures forever!" Amen! Amen!

Some people have raised a complaint against the ministers of the Church of England. Some of them have left the established church. But I must add that others who make this complaint are actually friends of that church. They say these ministers preach themselves and not Christ Jesus the Lord. They say the ministers give their people talks about mere morality and do not tell them the good news of salvation through Jesus Christ.

It is not my job to ask how well founded this complaint is. For now I will only say this. When such a serious complaint is made against the whole body of the clergy, every honest minister of Jesus Christ should do his very best. He should give no excuse at all to those who are looking for an excuse to take offense at us. They should hear us constantly proclaim the word of truth. They should hear us declare with full boldness and confidence of faith “that there is no other name given under heaven by which they can be saved except the name of Jesus Christ.” Then they may be ashamed of their confident boasting against us.

I had this complaint in mind. I was also drawn by how pleasant and delightful the subject is. (After all, who would not delight to talk about the very thing the blessed angels long to look into?) So I want to speak a little about a great and basic teaching of our faith. It is this: we are freely justified by the precious blood of Jesus Christ.
“But you are washed, but you are made holy, but you are justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”

These words begin with the word “but.” So they clearly point back to something that came before. Before I go into the details, then, it makes sense to look at how these words fit into the passage around them.

In the verses just before this, the apostle had listed many shocking sins, such as drunkenness, adultery, sexual immorality, and others like them. He tells the Corinthians that anyone who commits these sins without truly repenting from the heart will be completely shut out of God’s kingdom.

But the apostle saw two dangers. On one hand, they might become spiritually proud when they saw how different they now were from their unconverted brothers. Then they might look down on them and say, like the self-satisfied hypocrite in the prophet, “Keep away from me, for I am holier than you.” On the other hand, they might look back on all their past offenses and think their sins were too many and too serious to be forgiven. So first, to keep them humble, he reminds them of their sad condition before they were converted. He tells them plainly, “Some of you were like that” (or, as it could also be read, “these things were some of you”). In other words, some of you were once guilty, not of just one sin, but of that whole sad list of sins I have just described. But at the same time, to keep them from despair, he brings them good news of great joy: “But you are washed, but you are made holy, but you are justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”

I have already spoken to some extent about the first part of this text, about our being made holy. Now I want to speak more fully about our being freely justified by the precious obedience and death of Jesus Christ: “But you are justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”
From these words I will look at three things.
First, what the word “justified” means.
Second, I will try to prove that the whole human race, and every single person, needs to be justified.
Third, that there is no way to receive this justification we need so badly, except through the perfect obedience and precious death of Jesus Christ.
First, then, I will look at what the word “justified” means.

“But you are justified,” says the apostle. It is as if he had said, “Your sins are forgiven, and God now looks at you as if you had never offended him at all.” That is what the word “justified” means in almost every passage of holy Scripture where it appears.

For example, when this same apostle writes to the Romans, he tells them that “those whom God called, he also justified.” What comes next makes it clear that this word “justified” means all our wrongs are wiped out: “those he also glorified.” That could not happen if God did not look at a justified person as if he had never offended him at all.

Again, when he speaks about Abraham’s faith, he tells them that “Abraham believed in the one who justifies the ungodly.” That means God declares the ungodly person not guilty and clears him. It is a legal term. It pictures a judge who declares an accused criminal not guilty of the charge brought against him.
The apostle himself explains this expression with a quote from the Psalms: “Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord does not count against him.”
From all these proofs, and many others we could add, it is clear what being justified means. It means being cleared in God’s sight so fully that he looks at us as if we had never offended him at all.
That is also how we should understand the part of our creed that we say we believe, when each of us declares for himself, “I believe the forgiveness of sins.”
This brings me to the
Second point I promised: to prove that the whole human race, and every single person, needs to be justified.

In fact, the apostle already assumes this in the words of our text: “But you are justified.” By saying this, he implies that the Corinthians needed to be justified. And so does the whole human race, since there is no difference, as I will show later.

But I do not want to rely only on what is assumed. So as I explain this point further, I will try to prove that we all need to be justified for two reasons: because of the sin of our nature and because of the sin of our lives.
1. First, I say that we all need to be justified because of the sin of our nature. We are all guilty of original sin, the sin of our first parents.

A self-justifying unbeliever, who “will not come to Christ to have life,” may deny this. But no one who believes that St. Paul’s letters were written by God’s inspiration can ever deny it. For there we are told that “in Adam all died.” That means Adam’s sin was counted against everyone. And so that we do not forget to apply this to ourselves, another passage adds, “There is no one who does good (that is, by nature), not even one. We have all gone off the path (of original righteousness) and are by nature children of wrath.”

Even David was a man after God’s own heart. If anyone could claim to be free from this corruption that affects everyone, surely he could. Yet he confesses that “he was shaped in wickedness, and in sin his mother conceived him.”

Let me mention just one more passage, because it fits our purpose so well. In his letter to the Romans, St. Paul says that “death came upon all people because of the disobedience of one man, Adam. It came even upon those (that is, little children) who had not sinned the way Adam did.” These children had not committed any actual sin. So they could not have been punished with physical death unless the disobedience of our first parents had been counted against them. (This same apostle tells us elsewhere that death came into the world only through sin.)

So what I have said on this point is summed up very well in the article of our church that declares: “Original sin is not a matter of following Adam’s example. It is the fault and corruption of every person who is born naturally from the descendants of Adam. Because of it, people have gone very far from original righteousness and are inclined to evil by their own nature, so that the flesh always desires what is against the spirit. And so, in every person born into this world, it deserves God’s anger and condemnation.”

I have gone into this point in more detail because it is the very foundation of the Christian religion. I am truly convinced of this: many unbelievers oppose the faith, and many who call themselves Christians are very lukewarm in their love for Jesus Christ. The only reason is that they are not well grounded in the teaching of original sin. They do not see the helpless condition, indeed, I may say, the damnable condition, in which each of us comes into the world.
This is the reason, and I could almost say the only reason, why unbelief is so widespread among us.

Sadly, we are wrong if we think that people today become or remain unbelievers, and set up their corrupted reason against God’s revelation, simply because there is not enough evidence. (In fact, I believe it could easily be shown that a modern unbeliever is the most gullible creature alive.) No, the only reason is that they lack a humble mind. They have no sense of how corrupt they are by nature, and they are not willing to admit that they are so corrupt. That is why they stubbornly shut their eyes to the light of the glorious gospel of Christ.

But suppose they were once cut to the heart with a proper and living sense of their natural corruption and of the condemnation they face. Then they would no longer mock God’s revelation and treat it as a silly story. Instead, they would cry out like the trembling jailer, “What shall I do to be saved?”
A mistake on this basic point made so many people resist the evidence that the Son of God himself gave that God had sent him, when he lived among us.
Every word he spoke, everything he did, and every miracle he performed proved that he came from God.
So why did so many harden their hearts and refuse to believe his message?

He himself tells us why: “They will not come to me to have life.” They stubbornly resist the very means God had appointed for their salvation. And St. Paul tells us, “If the gospel is hidden, it is hidden to those who are lost. The god of this world has blinded the eyes of those who do not believe, so that the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, would not shine on them.”
2 Corinthians 4:3–4.
Someone may ask, “How does it fit with God’s goodness to count the guilt of one man’s sin against his innocent descendants?”
I think it would be enough to answer with the apostle’s words: “No, O man, who are you to talk back to God?
Should the thing that was made say to the one who made it, ‘Why have you made me like this?’”

But let me give a more direct answer. People would do well to remember that in the first covenant God made with humans, Adam acted as a public person. He was the representative of the whole human race. So we must stand or fall with him.

If he had kept on obeying and had not eaten the forbidden fruit, the benefits of his obedience would surely have been credited to us. But he did not keep on obeying. He broke the covenant that God made with him, and with us in him. So who would dare accuse the righteous Judge of all the earth of being unfair for counting that against us too? I will go on,
Second, to prove that we need to be justified because of the sin of our lives.

God made us, so he has the right to demand our obedience. I suppose no one will deny that. He has also given us two laws by which we will be judged: a natural law and a written law. No one who believes that St. Paul’s letter to the Romans comes with God’s authority can question this. For in that letter we are told about a law written in the heart and a law given through Moses. And our sad and frequent experience makes it all too clear that each of us has broken these laws.

So the holy Scriptures tell us that “there is no one who lives and does not sin,” that “we all do wrong in many things,” that “if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves,” and other things like this.

If we have offended God in this way, then we need forgiveness for offending him. The only other option would be to imagine that God makes laws but does not care whether they are obeyed. That is as foolish as imagining that a ruler would set up laws to govern his country well, and then let everyone who breaks them go unpunished.

But God has not acted so foolishly with his creatures. No, since he gave us a law, he demands that we obey it. He requires us to obey it in everything and to keep on obeying it. The penalty for every single breaking of it is nothing less than his curse and eternal death. That is what Scripture says: “Cursed is anyone who does not keep on doing everything written in the law.” And Scripture says in another place, “The soul who sins will die.”
Now I have already proved that all of us have sinned. So unless some way can be found to satisfy God’s justice, we must perish forever.
So let us stop for a moment. Let us see what a terrible condition each of us is born into, and stays in, until we are brought into a state of grace.

Surely nothing could be more terrible than to be born under God’s curse and to be charged with original guilt. And that is not all. We are also convicted of actually breaking God’s law, and even the smallest breaking of it rightly deserves eternal condemnation.
Surely this is a very sad way to see ourselves. It must make us try to find some way to satisfy and calm our offended Judge.
But what could that way be?
Shall we repent? Sadly, the first covenant does not say one word about repentance: “The day you eat from it, you will surely die.”
So if God is true, we must perish unless some way is found to satisfy his justice. And we have no reason to expect God to change his mind, even if we seek it with tears.
Well then, if repentance will not work, shall we appeal to the law of works?
Sadly, “no one living will be justified by the law, for the law brings the knowledge of sin.”
The law convicts and condemns us, so it can never justify us. And the prophet says, “All our righteous deeds are nothing but filthy rags.”
What then shall we bring when we come before the Lord and bow down before the Most High God?
Shall we come before him with year-old calves, with thousands of rams, or with ten thousand rivers of oil?

Sadly, God has shown you, O man, that this will do no good. For he has declared, “I will not take a bull from your house or a goat from your pen. For all the animals of the forest are mine, and so are the cattle on a thousand hills.”
Will the Lord then be pleased to accept our firstborn children for our wrongdoing, the fruit of our bodies for the sin of our souls?
Even this will not buy our pardon. For he has declared that “children will not bear the guilt of their parents.”
Besides, our children are sinners too. They are under the same condemnation, so they need forgiveness just as much as we do.
They are impure. And will the Lord accept the blind and the lame as a sacrifice?
Then shall some angel, or archangel, take on the task of keeping the covenant we have broken, and make atonement for us?

Sadly, they are only creatures, even if they are creatures of the highest rank. So they must obey God just as we must. And after they have done everything, they must say they have done no more than their duty.
And even if it were possible for them to die, how could the death of a limited creature satisfy a justice that has been offended infinitely?
What miserable people we are!
Who will rescue us?
I thank God, our Lord Jesus Christ.
This naturally brings me to the

Third point I promised. I will try to prove that there is no way to receive this justification we need so badly, except through the perfect obedience and precious death of Jesus Christ. “But you are justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

But I have already proved this to some extent in what I said under the last point. I showed that our repentance, our righteousness, and our sacrifices could never win justification for us. Not even the obedience and death of the angels themselves could do it. So all that is left for me to do under this point is to show that Jesus Christ has won it for us.
Here too I will turn “to the law and to the testimony.”

After all the clever arguments on both sides, only the living words of God can satisfy us on this very important point. It is such an unimaginable mystery that the eternal, one and only Son of God should die for sinful people. We would never have dared even to think of it if God had not revealed it in his holy word.
It is true that reason can show us the wound. But only revelation can lead us to the way we are healed.

God has chosen a certain way to make us happy. To the unbeliever it may be a stumbling block. To the self-important wise man and debater of this world it may be foolishness. But wisdom, that is, God’s plan of our redemption, will be proved right. All her truly wise and holy children, every sincere and honest Christian, will approve of it and submit to it.
But let me come more directly to our point.
As I said before, we needed two things in order to be at peace with God.
1. To be set free from the guilt of the sin of our nature.
2. To be set free from the sin of our lives.
And both of these are made certain for believers by the obedience and death of Jesus Christ. (Thank God for this gift that is too wonderful for words!)
For what does Scripture say?

1. About the first, it tells us that “just as through the disobedience of one man (that is, through one wrongdoing, Adam’s) many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one, Jesus Christ, many were made righteous.” (This includes both his passive and his active obedience.)

And again, “Just as through the disobedience of one man judgment came on all people and brought condemnation.” That is, all people were condemned because Adam’s sin was counted against them. “So through the obedience of one, Jesus Christ, the free gift of pardon and peace came on all people (all kinds of people) and brought justification that gives life.”

I say all kinds of people. In this chapter the apostle is only comparing the first Adam and the second Adam on one point: both of them acted as representatives. Adam’s descendants had his sin counted against them. In the same way, those for whom Christ died, and whom he represents, will have his merits counted as theirs.

Some people push this comparison further to prove that Christ redeemed everyone. Whatever arguments they may take from other passages of Scripture to prove this, if they try to use this passage for that purpose, I think they stretch their interpretation beyond what Scripture allows.
2. The other thing we needed to have made certain for us, before we could be at peace with God, was pardon for the sin of our lives.
And the holy Scriptures tell us that the death of Jesus Christ has fully done this.

The gospel prophet foretold that the promised Redeemer would be “wounded for our wrongdoings and bruised for our sins. The punishment that brings us peace would be on him, and by his wounds we would be healed,” Isaiah 53:6.
At his birth the angels said that he would “save his people from their sins.”
And St. Paul declares, “This is a trustworthy saying, and it deserves to be fully accepted by everyone: Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners.”

And here in the words of our text: “Some of you were like that (or, as I said before, these things were some of you); but you are washed,” and so on. And again: “Jesus Christ is the end of the law, bringing righteousness to everyone who believes.”

And the apostle St. Peter shows us that no one but Jesus Christ can do all this. He says, “There is salvation in no one else. For there is no other name under heaven given among people by which we must be saved, except the name of Jesus Christ.”
Then there are the Gentiles who still sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, on whom the sun of righteousness has never yet risen. How God will choose to deal with them is not for us to ask.
“What business is it of ours to judge those who are outside?”

Let us leave them to God’s mercy. And let us wait for the answer to this and every other hard question until the great day of judgment. On that day all of God’s ways, both in his providence and in his grace, will be made fully clear, in ways still unknown to us because they have not yet been revealed.
But this we do know: the Judge of all the earth will certainly do what is right.
But it is time for me to finish.
My brothers, by God’s blessing I have now spoken on the words of the text in the way I planned.
Many useful lessons could be drawn from what I have said. But I fear I have kept you too long already. So let me just make one or two reflections on what has been said, and then I will finish.

If we are freely justified by the death and obedience of Jesus Christ, then let us stop here for a moment. Before, we thought about the misery of a fallen soul. Now let us turn and look at the happiness of the believing soul.

But oh, I am lost in wonder when I think of it! When we were God’s enemies and rebels against him, God the Father still longed deeply for us, his fallen creatures who had turned away from him. Nothing but an infinite ransom could satisfy a justice that had been infinitely offended. So he sent his only and dear Son Jesus Christ, who is God, blessed forever, and who had been close to his heart from all eternity. He sent him to fulfill the covenant of works and to die a cursed, painful, and shameful death for us and for our salvation. Who can help crying out when thinking about this mystery of godliness?
“Oh, how deep are the riches of God’s love” for us, his wretched, miserable, and ruined creatures!
“How impossible it is to understand his mercy, and to trace out his ways!”
O God, now we truly know that you have loved us, “because you did not hold back your Son, your only Son Jesus Christ,” from doing all this and dying for us.
We admire the Father for sending his Son. Let us also humbly and thankfully worship the Son for coming when he was sent to die for mankind.

But oh! What mind can imagine, what words can express, how infinitely great that matchless love is? It moved the Son of God to come down from the dwelling places of his Father’s glory to obey and die for sinful people!
When he simply shed a tear at poor Lazarus’s funeral, the Jews said, “See how he loved him!”
How much more rightly, then, can we cry out, “See how he loved us!”
For he not only kept the whole moral law, but he did not hold back from shedding his own most precious blood for us.
After this, can any poor sinner who is truly convicted of sin give up hope of mercy?
Can such people see their Savior hanging on the cross, with his arms stretched out, ready to embrace them, and still doubt that he will accept them when they truly believe in him?
No! Get rid of all such thoughts. They dishonor him and lead to despair.

Look at his hands, pierced with iron nails. Look at his side, pierced with a cruel spear. It opened the floodgates of his blood and opened a fountain for sin and for all uncleanness. And then give up hope of mercy if you can!

No, just believe in him. Then, even though you have crucified him again, he will pardon you fully. “Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be like wool. Though they are deeper than crimson, they will be whiter than snow.”
May God in his infinite mercy grant this, etc.

This psalm is called the song of loves. These are the purest and most spiritual loves, the dearest and most delightful. They are the loves between Christ, the one who is loved, and his church, which is his bride. First, the psalm shows the Lord Jesus Christ in his majesty, power, and divine nature, and in his truth, gentleness, and fairness. Then it shows the bride: her jewelry, her friends, her servants, and the children who come after her. And it shows how lovely and beautiful both of them are.

After describing Christ, the psalm invites the human race to his wedding, and it calls them “daughter.” So it speaks especially to you, my dear sisters, because you are daughters of the human race. But that does not leave out the sons of the human race.
So now I will look at these words as spoken especially to you. They teach this truth:
